appraisal_events.evidence: Confident of election and largely indifferent to the post, the duc de Guermantes loses the Jockey Club presidency to the modest, unremarkable Chaussepierre, after a campaign built on claims the duchesse was a Dreyfusard and too close to the Rothschilds; 'l'obscurité triompha de l'éblouissement,' and the duke was left merely first vice-president.
appraisal_events.explanation: This surprise election defeat visibly and publicly diminishes the duke, who claims indifference but 'ne décolérait pas,' while the obscure Chaussepierre rises to a prestige neither his wealth nor social visibility would have predicted.

appraisal_events.evidence: When Oriane offers a reasoned counter-argument about why Jews might defend Dreyfus, the duke cuts her off with 'Les femmes n'entendent rien à la politique' and insists the matter is 'bel et bien une immense affaire nationale.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The duke peremptorily dismisses his wife's more measured argument on gendered grounds and reasserts his own dogmatic view, ending the exchange on his terms even as the narrator's mock-Jupiter framing keeps his pomposity in view.

status_effects.explanation: Losing a presidency he expected almost by right, to a socially obscure rival, is an explicit and painful public defeat within his own club world, even though he claims not to care.
A previously unremarkable, unostentatious figure is elected president of the Jockey Club over the preeminent duc de Guermantes, a witnessed rise that surprises everyone.
He cuts off Oriane's more reasoned point with a blunt dismissal and has the last word, ending the argument on his own dogmatic terms.
Her more measured counter-argument is peremptorily waved off with 'les femmes n'entendent rien à la politique,' leaving her silenced in front of company.

ambiguities: The narrator frames the duke's outburst with mock-Jupiter irony and ties it to his still-smarting Jockey Club loss rather than genuine conviction, so his rhetorical dismissal of Oriane may read as much as further exposure of his pettiness as a real rhetorical victory.
